| “Feedback not sent” with “Your draft is saved and was not discarded. …” | Try again right away. |
| “You sent several reports in a short time. …” | Wait a few minutes and then send. |
| “The server did not accept an attached file. …” | Remove the file. PNG, JPG, PDF, TXT and JSON of at most 2 MB are allowed. |
| “No more than 3 files.” or “No more than 2 MB per file.” | Choose fewer or smaller files. |
| “This file could not be read. …” | Choose the file again or pick another one. |
| The screenshot is missing in SubKit Desktop | The window was hidden, or the picture was too large. Send without a picture or attach your own. |

### The same over the HTTP API

`POST /v1/feedback` accepts a report. The route only works with a browser session and needs no permission of its own. It answers `201` with the fields `id`, `intake_item_id` and `replayed`. `replayed` is `true` when the same `client_request_id` was filed before.

Every field, limit and error code is listed in “Reference: desktop app, rules, schedules and problem reports”.

### Without signing in

On the sign-in page, **Report a problem** opens a short form: what happened, an email address for follow-up questions (optional) and a screenshot (optional, PNG or JPG of at most 2 MB). **Send report** files it without signing in.

Behind the form and the button in SubKit Desktop is `POST /v1/feedback/anonymous`. The route needs no session and no key and takes the same fields, plus `device_id` from SubKit Desktop and an optional `contact_email`.

- **Where it goes:** to the **Inbox** of the operator workspace, in the category `feedback`. The item names `anonymous` as its collector. Without an operator workspace the server answers `503 feedback_unavailable`.
- **What is removed:** the same as for a report from the Cockpit.
- **How many:** 3 reports in 10 minutes per address, 3 per desktop device and 60 for the whole server. After that the server answers `429` with `Retry-After`.
- **How large:** at most 6 MB for the whole request. The limits for each file stay the same, so a larger request is refused with `413`.
- **From another site:** a browser request from another site is refused with `403 csrf_rejected`.
- **Retry:** a repeated `client_request_id` returns the stored report, but still counts against the limits.

The service descriptor names the route as `clients.desktop.anonymous_feedback_path`.
## Cockpit branding

Branding makes the signed-in Cockpit show your name, your logo and a matching color palette instead of the SubKit look. You need it when your team should recognize the Cockpit as its own tool. Afterwards everyone signed in to your workspace sees the same look; login, email and other clients stay with SubKit.

### Change it in the Cockpit

A workspace is your tenant in the engine: its own data, its own users, its own permissions. To make changes you need `settings:write` and `identity:write` there. Under Settings → Operations, in the Appearance area (section Workspace branding), you set:

- the wordmark, meaning the displayed name, and an optional subtitle,
- one logo each for the light and the dark theme,
- one of three reviewed palette pairs.

The preview stays in your browser until you save. Reset restores the SubKit look. An accessible “powered by SubKit” attribution remains even with your own branding.

### What happens to uploaded logos

PNG, JPEG and WebP up to 2 MiB and 4 megapixels are accepted. SubKit decodes every image and stores it again as a still PNG of at most 512 pixels per edge; source metadata is dropped. SubKit refuses animation, SVG, external image addresses, scripts and custom CSS. The palette leaves the status colors unchanged, for example those that show errors or success.

Branding lives in your workspace's PostgreSQL schema. In hosted operation it counts against the storage quota.

### Through HTTP, CLI and MCP

Cockpit, HTTP API, `subkit` and MCP follow the same rules: the same image checks, the same permissions, the same revisions. Every saved version has a revision. If someone else has saved in the meantime, your save fails with a conflict and the saved version stays. Reload and try again.

Authenticated callers read with `GET /v1/tenant/branding`, save with `PUT` and reset with `DELETE`. Writing needs both permissions, `settings:write` and `identity:write`. A scoped API key stays limited to its permissions; browser writes additionally check the CSRF token. Logo reads are bound to the workspace and revision. If only one logo is stored, the Cockpit uses it for both the light and the dark theme; HTTP, CLI and MCP return both logo addresses.

The CLI offers these commands:

```bash
subkit branding get
subkit branding update <json-file|->
subkit branding reset <revision>
subkit branding logo <light|dark> --output <file>
```

MCP provides `get_tenant_branding`, `update_tenant_branding`, `reset_tenant_branding` and `get_tenant_branding_logo`. Changes through MCP need the usual approval by a signed-in person. SubKit checks both write permissions before it requests that approval. Ordinary reads return metadata; only `get_tenant_branding_logo` returns the normalized PNG bytes. The OpenAPI and MCP input schemas are generated from the same request definition.
## Installed Cockpit sessions

You can install your workspace's Cockpit as a web app on a phone or computer. It pays off when your team should get notifications by push or share files and text from other apps to SubKit. Afterwards the app has its own address, its own session and its own icon, and it checks the same permissions as the normal Cockpit.

### Create the installation

From a signed-in browser session you create the installation with `POST /v1/cockpit/installations` and an empty JSON object. If one already exists, SubKit reuses it. The request needs the usual browser CSRF token. The response contains the installation address and its manifest address, and the installation gets its own browser session. Your session in the normal Cockpit (root Cockpit) stays active.

There is exactly one web app installation per active workspace and owner on the current host; another workspace gets its own. Every computer with SubKit Desktop is, in addition, an installation of its own of the kind `desktop`. It is created when the app signs in, not through this route; more in “Operate the desktop sign-in”.

- `GET /v1/cockpit/installations` reads this owner's current installation without issuing a session. Under `installations`, the answer also lists every installation with `kind` (`browser` or `desktop`), `device_label`, `created_at`, `last_used_at` and `current`. The session of an installed app gets the list too; `installation` is then `null`.
- `DELETE /v1/cockpit/installations/{id}` revokes exactly that installation. The normal Cockpit offers the revocation of the web app in the workspace menu and that of every device under **Settings** › **Your profile** › **Where are you signed in?**. From inside an installed app only that app itself can be signed out.

### Session and sign-out

Each app runs under `/cockpit/i/{installationId}/` with its own cookie for exactly that path: HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax and, over HTTPS, also Secure. Under `/cockpit/i/{installationId}/api/v1/` the app reaches the same API as the normal Cockpit. The same handlers, permissions, CSRF checks, tenant-context checks and hosted quotas apply.

The server checks the session's owner, workspace, installation, expiry and revocation. An app session cannot switch workspace and never falls back to the normal Cockpit session. App event streams recheck the session before delivering each chunk.

This is how an app session ends:

- Signing out revokes only the presented session of this app.
- If you revoke the installation in the normal Cockpit, all its sessions become invalid. If you create it again, it gets a new identity; old links do not become valid again.
- Signing in again through OIDC (OpenID Connect, sign-in through an external identity provider) must return exactly the existing owner identity. It never creates an account and never links one by email address.
- An API key cannot renew an app session. Open the normal Cockpit instead and reopen the workspace app from there.

### App name and icon

The app manifest is only available when signed in and has its own ID, scope and start address. It uses the workspace's saved name, the palette and an optional square app icon. The uploaded icon must be square and at least 512 pixels per edge; the branding byte and pixel limits apply. SubKit generates 192 and 512 pixel PNGs from it. Without a custom icon, the manifest also ships the SubKit mark as a maskable and as a monochrome icon.

The manifest also carries three shortcuts (Chat, Tasks, Inbox) and registers the app for links with the `web+subkit` scheme, for example `web+subkit://tasks` or `web+subkit://chat/{id}`. Such a link opens the matching page in the app; unknown targets lead to the start page. If the app is already running, another launch brings the open window to the front.

Name, icon and manifest responses are private and never stored in an HTTP cache. Signed-out entry pages stay neutral. The browser or operating system may still keep an installed app's name and icon after sign-out.

### Without a connection and after an update

The app's service worker is a background script whose scope is exactly the installation path. It keeps the Cockpit's program files (the files under `/cockpit/assets/`, which are the same for every workspace), separately per installation and per server build. It never caches pages, API responses, workspace icons or private drafts, and it does not queue writes for later.

If the server cannot be reached, the app shows the page “No connection to the server” with “Try again” instead of a browser error. You do not see data without a connection.

After a server update the app detects the new build and offers “Reload”. Until then the open window keeps running on its previous build; unsaved input is not lost. On sign-out the app empties its cache and ends push on this device. If the installation is revoked, the app also removes its service worker the next time it is opened.

### Sharing and files

The service worker accepts a bounded amount of content that you send through “Share” from other apps.

Shared files and text stay in volatile memory until you explicitly confirm the import. Even then nothing happens on its own: uploading or collecting does not admit the source to knowledge, create a skill, call a model or start a workflow. Sources keep their original references. Local files and clipboard text are stored as a source artifact.

If the sign-in or the worker's volatile receipt is lost, share the content again after signing in or pick the file once more. The app checks file launch, clipboard and native file dialogs at runtime and uses them only after an explicit action by you. It never persists access to files or folders.

### Push in the installed app

You turn on push separately for each app and device. On the explicit preparation step, SubKit creates an encrypted VAPID key pair for your tenant, which the server uses to sign web push messages. Subscriptions are stored encrypted and bound to the installation and its owner.

A message arrives within about a minute when an item that needs attention is new or changes. Unchanged items do not notify again. The app shows one notification per item: the title says what happened (something was stopped, something is failing, a decision is waiting), the text says what to do. A click opens the item in the app or brings the open window there. It never contains names of workflows or connectors, branding, private content or approval actions. More than three items at once are folded into one generic hint.

The app icon carries the number of open items where the browser and operating system support it. When nothing is open any more, the number disappears.

When push ends:

- If an idle session expires, push stays on. When you reopen the app, the existing subscription is bound to the new session.
- Push ends on sign-out, on any explicit session revocation and when the installation is revoked.
- Push also ends when the owner is deactivated, the workspace is switched or deleted, and after 30 days without app use.
- Inactive or deleted owners and workspaces receive no new messages.

There are three limits to know. Messages already sent may still arrive after sign-out. The browser's notification permission may apply to all apps on the same origin (scheme, host and port of the address) and is not revoked automatically on sign-out. Path-bound sessions do not create their own origin, so browser storage and local permissions are not separated.

### Push in the normal browser Cockpit

The normal Cockpit at `/cockpit/` can also receive these notifications without an installation. The bell opens the same opt-in. When you turn push on, the browser asks for its permission. SubKit then registers the push-only worker at `/cockpit/sw.js` and binds the subscription to you and your workspace.

The same push routes accept a normal Cockpit session with a CSRF token. SubKit refuses API keys and bearer tokens, meaning credentials sent in the `Authorization` header. Installation paths never fall back to this session.

If an idle session expires, the subscription remains. After your next sign-in it applies to the new session without asking again. It ends:

- on sign-out, on an explicit session revocation or when you turn push off,
- when the workspace is switched or its lifecycle changes,
- when the user is deactivated or deleted,
- when the push endpoint expires or after 30 days without use.

Another user or workspace in the same browser must opt in again. Each device receives at most one message per change. If the installed app is enabled on the device, the message goes to the app and not to the browser tab. Browsers without push in a tab, such as Safari on iOS, offer installation as an app instead.
## Engine operator

An engine can hold several workspaces; one of them is the engine operator and administers the engine as a whole. You need this chapter when you change settings, maintain secrets or issue API keys. Afterwards you know which change applies to everyone and which only to your workspace.

### What only the operator may do

Technically, every workspace is its own tenant with separate data, users and permissions. The operator is the workspace that completed first-run setup (on a local development seed, `default`). Only its admins can read or change the whole engine:

- engine-wide settings and their revisions,
- runtime secrets and prepared secret approvals,
- engine restarts,
- engine diagnostics and logs, and `/metrics`,
- disabling an MCP OAuth client for every workspace.

In `GET /v1/rbac/permissions` these permissions carry `operator: true`: `settings:read:global`, `settings:write:global`, `system:restart`, `metrics:read` and `mcp_oauth_client:disable`. Outside the operator workspace, no role, grant or key scope can unlock them. Such a request answers `403` with `details.cause: "operator_only"`. `GET /v1/identity/whoami` reports `engine_operator` for this.

The operator workspace is chosen once. You can move it only on the host:

```bash
engine --set-operator-tenant <slug>
```

### Your workspace's settings

Every other workspace keeps its own settings. `GET /v1/settings` returns your tenant's view: only settings that support a per-tenant overlay, each with its effective value. A change applies to your workspace only when you name it explicitly:

```bash
subkit settings set llm.model '"<model>"' --tenant <your-tenant-id>
```

In the Cockpit, workspaces outside the operator currently see settings read-only. Use the CLI command above to make changes.

Without `--tenant` the engine refuses the change instead of applying it to everyone. While the operator has saved engine-wide settings that are not active yet, a workspace change answers `409 operator_change_pending` and is not saved. If you revoke an MCP OAuth client outside the operator, it loses access in your workspace only.

### Scopes for API keys and invites

A scope limits what an API key or invite may do. Allowed are scopes from the permission catalog, `*`, or the MCP modes `mcp:read`, `mcp:authoring` and `mcp:admin`. These rules apply:

- The issuing credential must hold every scope itself.
- Only a credential without scope limits can issue `*`.
- A key without scopes inherits the limits of whoever issues it.
- Rotating a key applies the same check to the scopes it already carries.

Unknown scopes answer `422 unknown_scope`, scopes beyond the issuer's permissions answer `403 scope_exceeds_issuer`.
## Execution identity and permission

Every run involves four separate things: who triggered it, how it signs in, what it may do and what a person approved. You need this chapter when a workflow should run only for particular signed-in people or apps, or when you want to attribute a run afterwards. Afterwards you know where to find a run's identity and which details cannot establish it.

### The four concepts

- `$caller` answers who authenticated this run.
- Connector credentials authenticate an outbound request to another service.
- RBAC, role-based access control, decides which workflows and resources that principal may use. A principal is the authenticated identity, meaning a person, an app or a key.
- A person's approval permits a reviewed reach of effect for an environment.

The four are independent. A credential or an approval does not create caller identity and does not replace authorization. The approver need not be the run's caller.

### Who the caller is

HTTP and MCP runs take the caller from their authenticated principal. Trusted callerless webhook and scheduled runs receive `null`. Whoever configured or approved them does not automatically become their caller. Child workflows keep the parent's caller.

If a workflow should run only for a particular authenticated identity, set `required_caller_kind` and `product_id`. Never infer that identity from input fields or `request_source`.

### Trace a run

Through HTTP and MCP every run shows source, status, workflow version, execution authority, step evidence and a safe summary under `caller`. It names the stored principal, product, authentication method, channel and origin run, but no credentials and no session identifiers. If the stored identity is missing, it shows `kind: unknown`; a channel alone does not identify a caller.

HTTP audit queries and MCP `list_audit` filter by actor and trace. These records correlate only partially and do not form a complete caller timeline. The exact rules and their limits are in the built-in Core Concepts, Auth Flows and REST API guidance.

### Task runs

A task is a goal with limits that SubKit works towards on its own. For a run of a task, the four concepts read like this:

- **Who it is.** A run acts as the owner of the task, also when a schedule started it and nobody is signed in. Every record of the run carries the access type “task run” with the task and the run, so you can tell it apart from what the owner did by hand.
- **What it may do.** The owner’s role is the upper bound. Within it, the run may only start the workflows and call the connectors bound to the task, in the environment of the task. It cannot create or change workflows, and it cannot start a workflow with `execution_privacy: sensitive`.
- **What a person approved.** A start by hand allows that one run. A start on a schedule needs the standing permission of the task. It is tied to the content of the task: any change to the goal, the plan, the bindings, the schedule, the limits or the environment ends it. A new name does not. Whether a bound workflow may write is decided by the approval of that workflow: when a valid one covers the start, the workflow writes without asking, also when the task has no standing permission. Otherwise its writes are held back and the run asks.
- **Who approved.** The standing permission is given by a person signed in to the Cockpit in the browser, the owner or an admin. That person is recorded as the approver and does not become the caller of the runs.

Before every background round, SubKit checks again that the owner is still active, the run is still open, the task is neither paused nor archived, and the standing permission of the run has not been revoked. If one of these fails, the round does not run.

A person who writes into a run does not widen it. The owner and admins can write; the same limits apply to their rounds. Writes that a run holds back are released by the owner or an admin. They are carried out with the permissions of the run, not with those of the admin, and the audit trail names the person who decided. A result is confirmed or sent back by a person signed in to the Cockpit in the browser, not with an API key, in `subkit` or from an AI client.

In the audit trail, background work of a run is recorded as the system with the scheduler or the queue as its source. Approvals, confirmations and stops name the person who acted. The entries hold identifiers, states and reason codes, never the goal text or an answer.

### In chat: draft, run and cost

If a saved draft changes while you work on it in chat, chat keeps your local edits. Saving, activating and running are separate steps with their own outcome. After you apply a draft in DEV, a single run with the recorded test inputs starts only when you tick **Start a run afterwards**. If you ask not to run live, this run does not happen. In PROD a live run needs an explicit request.

The recorded run shows what actually happened. The chat's model cost is an estimate from the provider's reported usage and the configured prices, not an invoice. The token count includes context that is sent repeatedly across model calls. Short release notes are under **Changes** in the lower-left account menu; unpublished changes are listed separately there.
## Product identity binding

With an identity binding, a user of your app who signs in through your own sign-in service lands on exactly one prepared account in SubKit. You need it when an app or customer portal should start selected workflows without its users getting full SubKit accounts. Afterwards every sign-in is bound to an account with minimal rights, and no new accounts appear on their own.

Three terms first. A product is your own app or service, which you mark in SubKit with `product_id`. OIDC (OpenID Connect) is a standard through which an external sign-in service, the issuer, confirms who signed in. The subject is the stable user identifier that this issuer provides.

### Prepare the account

For an OIDC provider configured with `product_id`, you as operator prepare the account first:

1. Create an active user in the tenant.
2. Give it a custom role with minimal rights.
3. Grant it only the intended saved workflows.

Do not use a built-in member role for this. It allows running considerably more workflows.

### Bind the subject

Bind the issuer's verified subject to this user:

```http
POST /v1/identity/users/{id}/provider-identities

{"provider_id":"<provider-id>","subject":"<verified-subject>"}
```

This requires administrator policy and `identity:write`. Tenant, issuer and product come from the provider configuration. An exactly repeated request changes nothing. If it conflicts with an existing binding on owner, subject, issuer or product, SubKit refuses it. The endpoint changes neither roles nor grants.

### What applies at sign-in

Product providers require this binding. They create no accounts and link none by email address, even when signup is enabled globally. For older product bindings, an operator must pin the same owner and subject before sign-in.

Providers without a product binding link by email address by default; `link_by_email: false` turns that off. Older bindings without a product pin the configured issuer at their first verified sign-in. That cannot establish which issuer applied earlier.

Pins are checked for new sign-ins. If you change the provider configuration, existing browser sessions stay valid. Revoke them separately or let their configured lifetime expire.
## Product bearer tokens and caller budgets

Your app can call SubKit with its own users' sign-in instead of shipping a SubKit key. You need this when a native app or portal starts workflows for signed-in customers. Afterwards SubKit verifies every token itself and creates a tightly limited account per user; per workflow you can also set a daily quota per user.

A bearer token is a credential the app sends in the `Authorization: Bearer …` header. Here it is a JWT (JSON Web Token): a signed data package whose issuer and content SubKit can verify. OIDC (OpenID Connect) is the standard through which SubKit finds the issuer's keys and details.

### Configure provider and product

Add a provider with `oidc_bearer` and an entry under `products` through runtime configuration. Hosts in the example are placeholders. `audience` and `required_claims` have no defaults; you state both for your issuer. The complete checklist is in the chapter "Onboard an app".

```json
{
  "auth": {
    "providers": [
      { "protocol": "api_key", "id": "api-key", "label": "SubKit API key" },
      {
        "protocol": "oidc_bearer",
        "id": "app-accounts",
        "label": "App account",
        "issuer_url": "https://idp.example.test",
        "audience": "app-audience",
        "algorithms": ["ES256"],
        "product_id": "app",
        "tenant_slug": "default",
        "required_claims": [
          { "path": "idp", "equals": "primary" },
          { "path": "claims.tier", "equals": "member" }
        ],
        "reject_anonymous": true,
        "clock_tolerance_s": 30
      }
    ]
  },
  "products": {
    "app": {
      "execution_environment": "prod",
      "assistant_workflow_id": "00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",
      "budget_bucket": "assistant"
    }
  }
}
```

`label` is only the provider's display name, in the example the app account ("App account"). A claim is a field in the token. `reject_anonymous` refuses tokens whose `is_anonymous` claim is true.

### How SubKit verifies the token

The app sends `Authorization: Bearer <access token>`. SubKit reads only that header, never a `token` query parameter. SubKit claims a token only when it is a compact JWS, meaning a signed JWT in the usual dot-separated form, and its `iss` equals a configured `issuer_url`. This provider never claims SubKit keys, portal tokens (short-lived SubKit tokens for embedded end-user runs), MCP tokens or exchanged tokens.

SubKit then verifies:

- the signature against the issuer's JWKS, meaning its published keys; it comes from `jwks_uri` or the OIDC discovery, is cached per provider and refetched once for an unknown key,
- the audience and the list of allowed algorithms,
- `exp`, `iat` and a `sub` in UUID format,
- every `required_claims` entry, where `path` is a dot path into the verified payload,
- anonymous subjects, when `reject_anonymous` is true.

If any check fails, SubKit answers `401 {"code":"unauthorized","error":"unauthorized","message":"invalid bearer token"}`. For that request SubKit then tries no other provider, cookie or key.

### What a product caller may do

On a subject's first verified token, SubKit creates a product user. It gets the built-in member role, a placeholder address and an identity binding to the provider, issuer and product; email addresses are never linked. The product ceiling leaves this principal, meaning the authenticated identity, only `workflow:run`, `execution:read` and `execution:abort`. These apply to saved workflows with the same `product_id` and to its own executions.

These limits also apply:

- No MCP surface: `/mcp` answers `403 product_caller_forbidden`, and the tool dispatcher refuses every tool outside those three permissions with `policy_denied`.
- `oidc_bearer` providers never issue API keys or browser sessions and are not listed for browser login.
- Runs always use the product's `execution_environment`; SubKit ignores an `x-subkit-environment` header for them.
- Runs of a product principal verified through `oidc_bearer` are always live. Without a live execution authority, an active version or a usable prepared credential, SubKit answers 403 with the refusal code.
- The run then does not start as a held preparation, meaning a preview with writes held back. `hold_writes: true` answers `403 product_preparation_forbidden`.

### Daily quota per caller

A sensitive product workflow with `required_caller_kind: "user"` may declare two guards:

- `execution_guards.caller_daily_limit` limits use per caller and day. Fields: `bucket`, `limit`, IANA `tz`, `unit` as a `$input` path, `lease_ms`, `billable_steps`, optional `meter` (JSONata), `max_metered`, `commit_when` (JSONata over the run output) and `attach_usage_as`.
- `execution_guards.input_bytes` limits the UTF-8 bytes per `$input` path. A string counts itself, other values count their JSON text.

Counting happens in units; `unit` decides which input value defines a unit. On admission SubKit first checks the sizes. It then reserves one unit per caller and local day, in the same transaction that creates the execution, and only after the idempotency replay check. A replay therefore never charges.

Later calls of a reserved or committed unit are free until `max_metered` calls were used. A unit runs only one call at a time. A call whose cancel was requested no longer counts as running. Refusals create no execution:

- `429 {"error":"rate-limited","code":"rate_limited","message":"…","usage":{"usedToday":50,"dailyLimit":50}}` when the day is used up,
- `409 {"error":"turn-busy","code":"turn_busy"}` while another run of the unit is queued or running; that run continues, and the same request with the same `idempotency_key` replays it (`idempotent_replay: true`, 202 while it runs) instead of reserving again,
- `429 {"error":"turn-limit","code":"turn_limit"}` once `max_metered` calls were used (every request a billable step sends counts when it is sent),
- `400 {"error":"invalid","code":"invalid"}` for an input part above its byte limit.

### Charge and refund

When a run ends:

- On success SubKit commits the unit if `commit_when` is true. Otherwise it stays reserved for the next call.
- As soon as a billable step sends its request, the unit counts as billable. This happens after the execution authority check. A failure, abort or timeout after that point stays charged.
- A failed, aborted or timed-out run gets the unit refunded only under three conditions: no billable request was sent, no billable step succeeded, and no other run of the unit is active.
- SubKit settles reservations whose lease expires on the next read: billable units are committed, the others refunded.

A successful run's sensitive result contains `usage: {usedToday, dailyLimit}`.

### Endpoints for product clients

- `GET /v1/budget` returns `{usedToday, dailyLimit, day, resetsAt}` for the product's assistant workflow.
- `GET /v1/health` returns `{ok, version, model, key}`. `ok` needs the active workflow, a live execution authority for the product environment and a usable credential on every connector it uses; no secret is read.
- Both answer 404 to principals without a product.
- `POST /v1/executions` with a `workflow_id` and no `source` runs that saved workflow. A product client therefore sends only `{workflow_id, idempotency_key, async, input}`.
- `GET /v1/executions/{id}` also returns `execution_id` and `error: {code}` for failed or timed-out runs.

An admin may create a workflow under a fixed `id` so an app can address it without configuration. The id must be unused.

### Erase the caller after success

`caller_erasure: "on_success"` on such a workflow erases the caller as soon as the run succeeds:

- Budget rows and identity bindings are deleted.
- Sessions and keys are revoked.
- The user is disabled and anonymised.
- The subject is removed from its executions' caller context.
- A tombstone holding only the subject's SHA-256 refuses tokens issued before the erasure.

Request steps can address the caller's own record with `${caller.subject}` and the boundary rule `{caller_bound: true}`. The rule is also accepted on a DELETE.

### Credentials of the step's own connector

A request step of a saved workflow may read its own connector's credential as `${cred.<own-slug>.<field>}` without `connector:read`. This applies only under a live execution authority and not in a held preparation. The reference must stay inside the approved reach. Draft and step runs, held preparations and saved runs without an authority still need `connector:read` on that connector.

The actual boundary: the credential is sent only to that connector's origin and never with a redirect. SubKit also redacts the raw, URL-encoded, form-encoded and JSON-escaped forms of the value from step outputs, errors, audit and logs. This is only a best-effort aid. If an upstream reflects the value in another encoding, or stores it and returns it later, it is not covered.
## Supabase-backed product workflows

With the `supabase` connector your product workflows reach your Supabase project without direct PostgreSQL access and without SQL steps. You need this when an app should read or change its users' data through SubKit. Afterwards every key sits encrypted on the connector, and you reach user-owned data through the verified caller instead of a user token passed along.

This section covers the `supabase` connector only. It does not matter which identity provider signs the app's users in. You author workflows as usual.

### Credentials on the connector

Store the required gateway headers as encrypted connector credentials:

- `apikey` is the public project key.
- `Authorization` carries the JWT (a signed token) for the intended database role.
- `x-subkit-token` may additionally be required by a protected server-to-server RPC. It is stored only on the connector and identifies SubKit to your product backend. It is not the end user's identity and never replaces the workflow's immutable `$caller`.

Do not use `service_role` for access on behalf of a caller: this role bypasses RLS, the database's row-level access rules. Never put credentials in app code, workflow inputs or steps, client context, generated workflow source, or logs.

### Data of individual users

A connector credential applies to the whole tenant and cannot represent separate mobile users. Never pass an app user's JWT as workflow input for that reason. When a workflow needs user-owned data, use an RPC, meaning a database function behind an endpoint, that derives the owner from the immutable `$caller`.

Bind product workflows to their product and the required caller kind. Derive owner identifiers from `$caller`. If an atomic authorization or quota reservation does not explicitly permit the next step, the workflow must fail closed instead of continuing.
## External MCP OAuth credentials

Some external MCP servers require an OAuth sign-in before SubKit may use their tools. You need this chapter when you set up such a server as a connector or want to keep using older saved sign-ins. Afterwards every sign-in is bound to a fixed authorization server, and client secrets go only there.

OAuth is the common method by which one service grants another access. The authorization server issues the tokens for it.

### Sign-in with client credentials

For connectors using `oauth2_client_credentials` or `oauth2_private_key_jwt`, enter the trusted authorization server URL as `config.mcp.auth.issuer` before connecting. Without that binding SubKit does not use the credentials. Discovery, the automatic lookup of server addresses, then cannot redirect a client secret or signed assertion to another authorization server.

### Interactive sign-in

With interactive MCP OAuth, SubKit stores the authorization-server issuer together with the encrypted client information and tokens. SubKit does not reuse older saved credentials without an issuer. For providers with dynamic client registration, you start a new sign-in through the connector's OAuth setup.

### Older credentials without dynamic registration

Whether older confidential clients at providers without dynamic registration can be recovered through the public setup APIs is not verified yet. Do not assume that entering an issuer afterwards restores those credentials. Put such connections into service only once their recovery has been verified. Do not edit stored credentials to bypass this check.

Changed discovery metadata does not migrate existing credentials. A new sign-in never inherits a refresh token issued by a different server. Review a provider change before you authorize it: the binding says nothing about whether a newly selected provider is trustworthy.
## Direct signed-JWT connector credentials

Some APIs, such as App Store Connect, expect a JWT signed with your private key instead of a password or OAuth token. You need this chapter when you set up such a service as a connector. Afterwards SubKit creates a fresh token for every request, and your private key sits only encrypted on the connector.

A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a short, signed data package; the recipient verifies it with your public key. Here SubKit sends it directly to the resource API in the `Authorization: Bearer` header. This differs from OAuth `private_key_jwt`: a direct signed JWT never goes to a token endpoint. SubKit creates it for the outbound request, retains it only in memory, and does not place it in a workflow, audit entry, or log.

The connector configuration holds the public signing policy: algorithm (`ES256` or `RS256`), audience, optional issuer, subject and key id. It also holds literal custom claims (fields in the token) and a 60–3600 second lifetime. The connector credential holds only the encrypted private key. SubKit supplies `iat` and `exp`; they cannot be set as custom claims. To rotate a key, replace the credential through the connector's normal credential screen, then verify it with the connector's authenticated test.

The built-in **App Store Connect** template is a direct signed-JWT connector for
`https://api.appstoreconnect.apple.com`. Its policy is fixed to `ES256`, audience
`appstoreconnect-v1`, and a five-minute lifetime.

Add the private `.p8` key as
the credential and configure the public Key ID. For a team key set the App Store
Connect Issuer ID as `issuer`; for an individual key omit `issuer` and set
`subject` to `user`. The first probe is `GET /v1/apps`. Do not configure OAuth,
a token endpoint, or an OAuth client assertion for this connector.

The template discovers endpoints from Apple's official OpenAPI ZIP download.
Discovery accepts a single JSON or YAML specification in an archive, limits
compressed and extracted content to 16 MiB, and rejects ambiguous archives.
The resulting endpoint catalog is available to agents; connector documentation
can also be imported with `POST /v1/connectors/{id}/docs/ingest` using
`source_type: "openapi"` and the extracted specification as `content`.

### Set up a signed-JWT connector

In Cockpit, under **Connectors**, choose **Add connector → From a template → App Store Connect**, then open the
connector's existing edit dialog. Enter the public Key ID and either the Issuer
ID (team key) or Subject `user` (individual key). Paste the private key into the
private-key field, save, and run the connector test. A saved key does not prove
that the provider accepts it; only a successful authenticated test does.

Use an App Store Connect API key that can read the intended apps and TestFlight
resources. A Sign in with Apple key is a different credential. The template
creates no testers, sends no invitations, and cannot bypass Apple's beta review.
It remains unverified in the catalogue until a real provider test has succeeded.

For other providers, the same HTTP or GraphQL connector mode accepts this public
configuration, without an Apple-specific transport or token exchange:

```json
{
  "auth_type": "signed_jwt",
  "config": {
    "signed_jwt": {
      "algorithm": "RS256",
      "audience": "https://api.example.com",
      "issuer": "service-account",
      "subject": "integration",
      "key_id": "provider-key-id",
      "ttl_seconds": 300,
      "claims": { "role": "reader" }
    }
  }
}
```

This is the auth part of a connector definition, not a complete create
request. Set the connector name, driver, environment and base URL as usual.
For GraphQL, set its endpoint through the existing GraphQL configuration. Public
claims must match the provider's documented requirements.

The App Store template fixes algorithm, audience, custom claims and lifetime. To change
them, you must explicitly clear or replace the template binding. SubKit checks public identity or key changes
against existing execution authorities.

Attach or replace the key to an already configured connector through the CLI:

```sh
subkit vault attach <connector-id> --mode signed_jwt --json < ./provider-key.p8
```

The CLI reads the file locally and sends its contents only to the authenticated
credential endpoint. The JSON result includes the probe outcome; a failed probe
exits unsuccessfully. `--skip-checks` skips the test and makes no connectivity claim.
Never paste a key into a command argument, connector config, workflow, or chat.
The credential API accepts `{ "mode": "signed_jwt", "private_key": "<PEM>" }`
and returns the credential ID, never the key or a generated token.

Keys must be unencrypted PKCS#8 PEM: P-256 for ES256, or RSA 2048–4096 bits for
RS256. SubKit encrypts stored keys, generates a fresh token for each actual
request attempt, and regenerates tokens after restart without a refresh job.
When setting up a draft, SubKit holds the submitted key only transiently in the protected
credential flow until it is saved; it never ends up in chat messages.
Requests cannot redirect to a different resource, and connector hooks do not see
the generated token. Reflected tokens are removed from provider results.

| Problem | Next action |
| --- | --- |
| Private key is invalid or has the wrong algorithm | Use the matching provider-issued PKCS#8 key. Do not submit a certificate, public key, JWK or generated JWT. |
| Provider returns 401 | Check Key ID, issuer/subject, audience, revoked keys and the engine's clock. Replacing a key does not fix an incorrect identity. |
| Provider returns 403 | Check the API key's provider role and access to the intended resource. |
| Provider redirects or target origin differs | Use the final documented API origin in the connector. Signed requests do not follow redirects. |
| Provider is unavailable | Retry the read-only test after recovery; do not replace a valid key solely for a temporary outage. |
| Key rotation | Update the public identity fields if needed, replace the private-key credential, then rerun the read-only test. Never reuse a previously generated JWT. |

### Rules for agents with signed JWTs

Discover the template before authoring a connector. Configure only public fields
under `config.signed_jwt`. Request the private key through SubKit's existing
sensitive credential form or browser setup handoff. Never request it in free-text
chat, and do not generate, print or store JWTs yourself. The secure form field is
`private_key`; `token` and OAuth `client_secret` are not substitutes.

After saving, read the authenticated probe result and report provider failures
without claiming connectivity. Check fresh build/review state before saying an
invitation can be used. An invitation or any other provider mutation requires its
own authorized workflow; the connector setup test performs only a read.

Use the generated OpenAPI schemas as the machine-readable specification and the template-bound
`app-store-connect-basics` skill for vendor guidance. The generated `/llms/setup.md`,
`/llms/connectors.md`, `/llms/cli.md` and `/llms-full.txt` ship with the engine and
are regenerated from these sources; do not maintain a second auth specification.

## Sandbox data tools

In a JavaScript transform step you calculate, parse and validate data with the built-in `sk` helpers. You need them when a workflow calculates amounts, reads CSV or XML, converts times across time zones or validates input. Afterwards you know what each helper does and where its limits are.

The helpers run synchronously and bounded inside the sandbox, the isolated runtime of the step. They never access the network, filesystem or credentials. Their namespaces are immutable. Promises and unseeded randomness are unsupported; for repeatable values use the execution clock and `sk.uuid()`.

| Task | Helpers | Rules |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decimal amounts | `sk.money.add/sub/mul/div/round/compare` | Decimal strings; `div` and `round` require scale and `down`, `halfUp`, `halfEven` or `up`. No currency conversion. |
| CSV | `sk.csv.parse/stringify` | Explicit delimiter/header options; export escapes spreadsheet formulas by default. Up to 10,000 rows. |
| Dates | `sk.date.parse/format/add/startOf/convertZone` | Date-only values stay dates. Local datetimes require an IANA zone; ambiguous or missing DST times require explicit `earlier`/`later`. |
| Validation | `sk.schema.validate/assert`, `sk.assert` | Local schema references only; no remote resolution or asynchronous validators. |
| URLs | `sk.url.parse/build/query/encode/decode` | WHATWG parsing, repeated query entries, UTF-8 percent encoding. No requests. |
| XML | `sk.xml.parse/build` | Ordered `{name, attributes, children}` trees retain mixed text; no DTD or custom entities. |
| Text and records | `sk.template.render`, `sk.diff.records` | Escaped HTML by default, explicit text mode; bounded list sections. Record diff requires a unique key. |

```javascript
return {
  total: sk.money.add("19.90", "4.95"),
  csv: sk.csv.stringify([{ name: "Ada", amount: "24.85" }]),
  tomorrow: sk.date.add("2024-02-28", 1, "days"),
  greeting: sk.template.render("Hello {{name}}", { name: "Ada" })
};
```

### Limits and operation

Text inputs and outputs are limited to 1 MiB, structures to 100,000 nodes and
64 levels. Existing sandbox memory, execution and output budgets still apply.
Each helper is embedded and loaded only on first access in each sandbox.
Package versions and timezone data are pinned for each release. The helpers do not
bring document rendering, OCR or a browser.

JavaScript transforms, JSONata and binary parsing run in bounded worker processes.
The default lane runs up to two workers in parallel; hooks have a separate lane.
Per engine process, global and per-tenant queue limits apply across both lanes.
On Linux an RSS watchdog polls memory use regularly.
It is not a kernel-enforced memory ceiling.
## Operate the desktop sign-in

This chapter is for anyone who runs a SubKit server and wants to offer SubKit Desktop to their team.
Afterwards you know what your server tells the app, which two settings you can set, how the sign-in works and how to revoke a device.
“SubKit Desktop” describes how people use the app.

### What you need

- An engine of version 12.1.0 or later. The update runs the migrations for the app’s sign-in.
- An address with `https://`. The app only connects over `https`; it allows `http` for `localhost` alone.
- A working way to sign in to the Cockpit in the browser. The app uses exactly this sign-in and no API key.
- The app itself. SubKit Desktop runs on a Mac with Apple Silicon and macOS 13 or later; the Windows app is coming soon. [Download it for Mac](https://github.com/MikeBild/subkit/releases/latest/download/subkit-desktop-mac-arm64.dmg); the link always serves the newest release. To build and distribute it yourself, see below. The Cockpit as an installed web app works on every system.
- For the local capabilities (files, browser and apps on the Mac) an engine of version 12.1.0 or later.

### What the server tells the app

Before every connection the app reads `GET /.well-known/service-descriptor.json`. The section `clients.desktop` tells it whether and how it can sign in.

```json
{
  "version": "<version>",
  "clients": {
    "desktop": {
      "min_version": "0.1.0",
      "login": {
        "start": "/v1/identity/desktop-login/start",
        "session": "/v1/identity/desktop-session",
        "callback": "subkit://callback",
        "callbacks": ["subkit://callback"],
        "code_challenge_methods": ["S256"]
      },
      "feedback_path": "/cockpit?feedback=1",
      "anonymous_feedback_path": "/v1/feedback/anonymous"
    }
  }
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `version` | The version of the engine. The app requires at least 12.1.0. |
| `clients.desktop.min_version` | The oldest app version this server accepts. An older app asks for an update instead of signing in. |
| `clients.desktop.login.start` | The address the app opens in the browser. |
| `clients.desktop.login.session` | The address where the app exchanges its code for a session. |
| `clients.desktop.login.callback` | The target the browser hands back to after the confirmation. |
| `clients.desktop.login.callbacks` | Every target this server accepts. An app whose target is missing does not sign in. |
| `clients.desktop.login.code_challenge_methods` | The accepted methods. There is only `S256`. |
| `clients.desktop.feedback_path` | The Cockpit address that opens the “Report a bug” dialog. |
| `clients.desktop.anonymous_feedback_path` | The route that takes a report before the app is signed in, see “Report a bug”. |

When `clients.desktop` is missing, the app reports the server as too old. When `login` is missing in it, the app reports that the server does not offer the sign-in it needs.

### The two settings

Both are in the Cockpit under **Settings** and apply to the whole engine, without a restart.

| Setting | Shown in the Cockpit as | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `server.desktop_min_version` | **Minimum desktop app version** | `0.1.0` | Published as `clients.desktop.min_version`. Format: three numbers such as `12.1.7`. |
| `server.desktop_dev_callback` | **Accept desktop development builds** | `false` | Also accepts `subkit-dev://callback` as a target. Outside `NODE_ENV=production` this applies without the setting. |

This is how you raise the minimum version:

1. Distribute the new app to your team first.
2. Set `server.desktop_min_version` to that version.
3. People with an older app read “The server requires at least version … of the app and you have ….” the next time they connect.

The app and the engine both enforce the minimum version. The app checks the published value when it connects. The engine checks the version the app names at sign-in as `app_version`, in three places:

| Place | Answer for an older app or without `app_version` |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /v1/identity/desktop-login/start` | `426` with a page “SubKit Desktop is out of date” that names the minimum version, and the header `X-SubKit-Error: desktop_app_outdated`. No sign-in is started. |
| Confirmation page, when shown and when submitted | The same page with `426`. No code is issued. |
| `POST /v1/identity/desktop-session` | `426` with the code `desktop_app_outdated`. The sign-in code is not consumed. The app shows “This version of the app is too old for this server. …” |

A pre-release such as `12.1.7-beta.1` counts as older than `12.1.7`. The check applies to new sign-ins: an older app that is already signed in keeps its session until it expires or you revoke the device. The app names its version itself; the limit keeps honest older apps out and does not replace access control.

Leave `server.desktop_dev_callback` switched off in production. Development builds are called “SubKit Dev”, use the scheme `subkit-dev://` and are meant only for developing the app.

### How the sign-in works

1. The app opens `GET /v1/identity/desktop-login/start` in the browser with a PKCE challenge (`S256`), a `state`, the ID and name of the device, and its version as `app_version`.
2. The engine redirects to the confirmation page. If the person is not signed in in the browser, they sign in as usual first.
3. The page names the device, the workspace and the account. The person selects **Sign in** or **Cancel**.
4. With **Sign in**, the browser hands back to `subkit://callback` with a code. With **Cancel**, it hands back `error=access_denied`.
5. The app exchanges the code for a session with `POST /v1/identity/desktop-session`, its `code_verifier` and its `app_version`. The answer sets an HttpOnly cookie for `/cockpit/i/{installationId}/` and never contains an API key.

What applies:

| Rule | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Validity of the confirmation page | 10 minutes |
| Validity of the code | 60 seconds, usable once. Any attempt consumes it. |
| Binding of the code | To the challenge, the workspace, the person and the device. A new code for the same device invalidates older ones. |
| Limit per address | 30 calls per minute for the start, 30 for the confirmation, 10 for the exchange. After that `429` with `Retry-After`. |
| Exchange from a web page | Refused with `403 cross_origin_rejected`. Only the app itself can exchange. |
| Confirmation from another site | Refused with `403 csrf_rejected`. |
| Workspace switched or signed in again after the page opened | The page opens again for the current workspace. Nothing is issued until you confirm once more. |
| Workspace context of the browser | Not required. The page always shows the workspace of the current browser session, even when a Cockpit tab has another workspace open. |

The engine counts the limits in the database. They apply across all engine processes together and survive a restart.

### How long a desktop session lasts

| Rule | Desktop device | Browser and installed web app |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Without use | 30 days. Any request of the app, also the open event stream, starts the period again. | 8 hours |
| At most since the sign-in | 90 days | 24 hours |
| Revoking the device, **Sign out**, a deactivated person | Ended at once | Ended at once |

The cookie of the desktop session lasts 90 days; whether the session still holds is decided by the engine on every request. After it expires the engine answers `401`, and the app asks for a new sign-in in the browser. The periods are fixed and not a setting. Approvals that require a live session of the person also accept the desktop session within these periods.

### View and revoke devices

Every computer is an installation of its own of the kind `desktop` with its own session. The same device ID reuses its installation; a new computer gets a new one.

The Cockpit shows a person’s devices under **Settings** › **Your profile** › **Where are you signed in?** and revokes them there after a question that names the device and the consequence. You can use the same routes directly. They accept a session of the Cockpit, with its CSRF token, and no API key. A person sees and revokes only their own devices with them:

| Route | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /v1/cockpit/installations` | Lists up to 50 of your own installations under `installations`, with `id`, `kind` (`browser` or `desktop`), `device_label`, `created_at`, `last_used_at` (the last request a session of this installation made, else `null`) and `current` (`true` for the installation the request comes from). |
| `DELETE /v1/cockpit/installations/{installationId}` | Revokes the installation. Answers `204`. The session of the normal Cockpit in the browser revokes any of your installations; the session of an installation only itself, otherwise `403 own_installation_only`. |

What the revocation does:

- All sessions of the device end, and its push ends.
- The engine checks the session of open event streams every three seconds. The app therefore learns of the revocation within a few seconds and signs out locally.
- Later requests with the old cookie get `403 installation_revoked`. An expired session gets `401 installation_session_required` instead; the profile then stays in the app, and the person signs in again.
- When the person signs in again on the computer, a new installation is created.

**Revoke installation** in the workspace menu only revokes the installed web app. The dialog says so: desktop devices stay signed in and are signed out under **Settings** › **Your profile**. Each installation is revoked on its own; there is no revocation of all devices at once.

When a person is deactivated, the exchange refuses with `403 user_inactive`.

### Build and distribute the app

Most teams use the signed builds from the [latest release](https://github.com/MikeBild/subkit/releases/latest). This section is for building your own from the repository. The app lives there under `apps/desktop`. A build for distribution is made there with `bun run package`. The repository does not bring the following; you supply it yourself:

| For | What you provide |
| --- | --- |
| Signing for macOS | A Developer ID certificate and the credentials for notarization. |
| Signing for Windows | A code signing certificate (Authenticode) with a timestamp, or a cloud signing service. |
| Updates | A place where you publish versions over `https`, and the decision to enable updates (`SUBKIT_DESKTOP_UPDATES=1` when building). |

Without enabled updates the app shows “Automatic updates are not enabled in this build.” An unsigned app cannot update itself, on macOS or on Windows. None of these values belongs in the repository. The details are in the README file under `apps/desktop`.

### What the audit trail records

| Action | When |
| --- | --- |
| `desktop_login.code_issued` | The person confirmed the device in the browser. |
| `desktop_login.denied` | The person cancelled (`declined_by_user`), or the exchange failed, for example `replayed`, `expired`, `invalid_verifier`, `state_mismatch` or `user_inactive`. |
| `desktop_login.completed` | The app received its session. |
| `cockpit_installation.created` | A new device was created, with `kind`, device ID and name. |
| `cockpit_installation.revoked` | A device was revoked, with the number of sessions ended. |
| `session.revoked` | Per session ended, with the reason `installation_revoked`. |

An exchange with an unknown code only appears in the engine log, not in the audit trail. The Cockpit so far shows the three `desktop_login.*` actions with their technical name.

### If something does not work

| What you see | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| The app reports the server as too old | Check `version` in the service descriptor. The app needs 12.1.0 or later and the section `clients.desktop`. |
| The app reports that the server does not offer the sign-in it needs | The app is a development build and your server does not accept `subkit-dev://callback`, or `login` is missing in the descriptor. |
| `400 invalid_redirect_uri` at the start | The app’s target is not in `callbacks`. Use a production build or switch on `server.desktop_dev_callback`. |
| `401 invalid_grant` at the exchange | The code is unknown, used, expired or does not match the `code_verifier`. The person starts the sign-in again. |
| `429` during the sign-in | Too many attempts from one address. Wait for the time in `Retry-After`. |
| The browser does not return to the app | The system does not know the scheme `subkit://`. Install the app again so that it registers it. |
| `401 browser_session_required` when listing devices | The route accepts only a session of the Cockpit and no API key. |
| `403 own_installation_only` when revoking | The request comes from an installation and names another one. Revoke the other device in the browser. |
| `426 desktop_app_outdated` at sign-in | The app is older than `server.desktop_min_version` or names no version. Update the app. |
